blocks.text: Consider a mass m attached to the end of a massless rod (Fig. 3.15), with a frictionless bearing at the pivot O and the system in a horizontal plane. A force F acting on the mass perpendicular to the rod accelerates it according to F = ma, and in doing so makes the mass rotate about O. Since the tangential acceleration a_T is related to the angular acceleration alpha by a_T = r alpha, F = m r alpha. As the turning effect is produced by torque tau, it is better to write the equation for rotation in terms of torque, by multiplying both sides by r: rF = tau = torque = m r^2 alpha, which is the rotational analogue of Newton's second law F = ma: F is replaced by tau, a by alpha and m by m r^2.

blocks.title: Moment of inertia
blocks.text: The quantity m r^2 is known as the moment of inertia and is represented by I. The moment of inertia plays the same role in angular motion as mass in linear motion. It depends not only on the mass m but also on r^2.

Most rigid bodies have different mass concentrations at different distances from the axis of rotation, so the mass distribution is not uniform. As in Fig. 3.16a, a rigid body is made up of n small pieces of masses m1, m2, ... at distances r1, r2, ... from the axis of rotation O. Let the body rotate with angular acceleration alpha; the magnitude of the torque acting on m1 is tau1 = m1 r1^2 alpha, similarly the torque on m2 is tau2 = m2 r2^2 alpha, and so on. Each small piece of mass within a large rigid body undergoes the same angular acceleration about the pivot point; since the body is rigid, all the masses rotate with the same angular acceleration alpha. The total torque is tau_total = (m1 r1^2 + m2 r2^2 + ... + m_n r_n^2) alpha = (sum from i = 1 to n of m_i r_i^2) alpha, or tau = I alpha ... (3.18), where I is the moment of inertia of the body, I = sum from i = 1 to n of m_i r_i^2 ... (3.19).

blocks.text: Of two cylinders of equal mass, the one with the larger diameter has the greater rotational inertia (Do You Know).

blocks.prompt: What is the moment of inertia of a 200 kg sphere of diameter 60 cm (numerical problem 3.6)? Mass measures inertia in linear motion; what is its analogue in rotation, and why does it depend on more than the mass (short question 3.4, MCQ 3.10)?
blocks.explanation: I = (2/5) m r^2 = (2/5) x 200 kg x (0.30 m)^2 = 7.2 kg m^2 (the printed answer 28.8 kg m^2 corresponds to using the diameter 0.60 m as r). The analogue is the moment of inertia I = sum m_i r_i^2, which measures the resistance to angular acceleration (tau = I alpha); it depends on the mass and on how that mass is distributed about the axis, since each piece contributes m_i times the square of its distance.

items: Mass on a rod: F = m r alpha, so rF = tau = m r^2 alpha; the rotational form of F = ma with I = m r^2 in place of m.

Rigid body of n pieces, all with the same alpha: tau = I alpha (3.18), I = sum m_i r_i^2 (3.19); I depends on mass and its distance from the axis. Rod (1/12) m L^2, hoop m r^2, disc (1/2) m r^2, sphere (2/5) m r^2.
